title: Valentines Day

jokes.text: Pam's talking head: 'Like last year, Jim gave me this card with Dwight's head on it. It was horrifying and funny.'
jokes.setup: Pam is describing a sweet Valentine's Day office tradition of giving presents
jokes.punchline: 'It was horrifying and funny' — the juxtaposition of a gruesome image with a sincere, affectionate recollection perfectly captures Jim and Pam's relationship dynamic
jokes.explanation: This opener does a lot of work efficiently. 'Horrifying and funny' is an oddly honest, warm reaction that immediately characterizes both Jim's pranking sensibility and Pam's genuine fondness for him. It's character-specific and economical — a lesser show would spell out the joke.

jokes.text: Phyllis's enormous Valentine's card reads 'Happy Valentine's Day, Darling, love Bob Vance, Vance Refrigeration' — he signs it with his company name
jokes.setup: Phyllis is receiving a romantic Valentine's card from her boyfriend
jokes.punchline: The card is signed 'Bob Vance, Vance Refrigeration' — an absurdly corporate sign-off on a love note, establishing the running gag of Bob always identifying himself by his business
jokes.explanation: The joke is precise and character-specific. Bob Vance signing a love card with his company name is absurd but completely in character and functions as the first seed of a running gag throughout the episode. 'Vance Refrigeration' as a recurring punchline is one of the show's great background jokes.

jokes.text: Michael asks Dwight to come to New York. Dwight: 'And you want me to come with you.' Michael: 'No. Opposite of that.'
jokes.setup: Dwight assumes Michael is inviting him along to New York since Michael always values his company
jokes.punchline: 'No. Opposite of that.' — blunt, economical rejection that punctures Dwight's presumption
jokes.explanation: The economy of 'Opposite of that' is what elevates this above a basic dismissal. It's a clean, quick laugh rooted in Michael's blunt self-absorption. Works because Dwight's presumption is so perfectly calibrated.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head: 'It's New York, city of love.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is advising Michael about Valentine's Day and Jan in New York
jokes.punchline: Dwight confidently misattributes 'City of Love' (Paris) to New York — delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: A small, clean joke relying on Dwight's confident ignorance. Works but isn't especially inventive — misattributing 'City of Love' is a well-worn comedic move. Redeemed by economy and Dwight's earnestness.

jokes.text: Michael to Pam: 'Hey Pam, you heart NY, right? You want me to pick you up anything?' then immediately pivots to 'Fo'get abou' it!' and a New York accent
jokes.setup: Michael is excited about going to New York and trying to perform his New York persona
jokes.punchline: 'Fo'get abou' it!' — an embarrassingly enthusiastic, completely unprompted New York affectation that reflects Michael's tendency to perform rather than simply exist
jokes.explanation: Functional Michael character comedy — his performative 'New York guy' routine. Not particularly fresh as a joke type but lands because Carell commits. 'Me in New York? Oh, I own that city' has good arrogant delusional energy.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'The city so nice, they named it twice. Manhattan is the other name.'
jokes.setup: Michael is explaining the 'New York, New York' saying to the camera
jokes.punchline: He thinks 'Manhattan' is the second name they're referring to — completely misunderstanding the expression while confidently explaining it
jokes.explanation: This is a great Michael joke. The expression 'the city so nice, they named it twice' is well-known, and Michael's confident explanation that the second name is 'Manhattan' is a specific, original misunderstanding. It's not random stupidity — it has an internal (wrong) logic that's distinctly Michaelian. Quotable and rewatchable.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head: 'So I broke up with Katy and haven't been dating anybody else. So this year I don't have to worry about Valentine's Day.'
jokes.setup: Jim frames being newly single on Valentine's Day as a positive — freedom from obligation
jokes.punchline: The audience knows from context (and Jim's lingering feelings for Pam) that this is sad rationalization presented with forced cheerfulness
jokes.explanation: The joke is partly verbal (Jim's forced positivity) and partly tonal — the audience reads the subtext of Jim's loneliness. Works on rewatch when you know more context. The poker game punchline ('I'll end up winning a lot of money because they're idiots') saves it from being too melancholy.

jokes.text: Dwight discovers a mysterious gift on his desk and interrogates it: 'What's this? What is this?... Yeah, but who put it here and for what purpose?'
jokes.setup: A Valentine's gift has appeared on Dwight's desk
jokes.punchline: Dwight's suspicious, forensic response to a romantic gesture — 'for what purpose?' — treating a gift as a threat or intelligence operation rather than a romantic expression
jokes.explanation: 'Who put it here and for what purpose?' is perfectly Dwight — romantic gestures processed through a security-threat framework. Character-specific and efficient. The setup of a mysterious gift is straightforward but the execution is strong.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head: 'It's me. I'm the bobble-head.' — delivered with barely contained joy
jokes.setup: Dwight received a bobble-head of himself as a Valentine's gift from Angela
jokes.punchline: Dwight's reaction is pure, uncomplicated delight — not 'I have a secret admirer' or 'I wonder who sent this' but the immediate and complete identification with the bobble-head. It's also inadvertently revealing that Angela got him something deeply specific to his narcissism
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. 'It's me. I'm the bobble-head.' is perfect in its economy and character specificity. After all the paranoid interrogation, Dwight's emotional response isn't gratitude, romance, or suspicion — it's pure self-recognition and pride. The line could only be said by Dwight. The pause before it (the [03:02]-[03:14] gap) lets the camera hold on Dwight experiencing the revelation. It's a joke that also doubles as a touching character moment, which is the show at its best. Qualifies for an 8+ score because of exceptional economy, complete character integration, and genuine originality in the specific type of delight expressed.

jokes.text: Michael's New York tour: 'Right here is my favorite New York pizza joint. And I'm gonna go get me a New York slice.'
jokes.setup: Michael is excitedly touring his 'favorite haunts' in New York before the big meeting
jokes.punchline: The implication (confirmed by later scenes) is that Michael's 'favorite haunts' are tourist traps — a pizza place that likely isn't authentically New York in any meaningful way, delivered with the pride of a true local
jokes.explanation: A setup joke for what's coming — Michael's tourist-as-local conceit. Functional but the punchline is implicit rather than delivered, so it depends on what follows. On its own, it's mild.

jokes.text: Kelly's rapid-fire recap of her night with Ryan, ending with: 'I mean, I just said it to him. Can you believe that?' Jim's face during this monologue.
jokes.setup: Kelly ambushes Jim with an extremely detailed account of her Valentine's hookup with Ryan
jokes.punchline: Jim's increasingly pained attempts to appear supportive while being overwhelmed by Kelly's enthusiastic oversharing — culminating in his polite 'No, don't be [embarrassed]' just to make it stop
jokes.explanation: Kelly's stream-of-consciousness is true to the character — the joke is the pace, the density of information, and Jim being trapped. The line 'Ryan, what took you so long?' being both an internal thought AND what she said out loud is a nice small gag within the larger scene.

jokes.text: Ryan's talking head: 'I hooked up with her on February 13th.'
jokes.setup: Kelly has been enthusiastically describing their Valentine's Day romance, implying it's deeply meaningful
jokes.punchline: Ryan's cold, flat correction — 'February 13th' — showing he's already creating distance from the Valentine's Day framing, making it explicitly not-romantic
jokes.explanation: This is an outstanding joke. The juxtaposition structure — Kelly's breathless romantic narration immediately cut against Ryan's one-line timestamp correction — is impeccably executed. 'February 13th' does enormous work: it's technically true, it precisely deflates Kelly's narrative, and it reveals Ryan's entire character and relationship to Kelly in four words. The joke earns its 8+ score through exceptional structure (the cut is perfectly timed), character specificity (only Ryan would think this way), and economy (no words wasted). One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: Times Square tour: 'Named for the good times you have when you're in it.'
jokes.setup: Michael is giving a confident tour of Times Square to the camera
jokes.punchline: Times Square is named for the New York Times newspaper — Michael's confident false etymology ('good times') is both wrong and oddly logical-sounding
jokes.explanation: Another confident Michael misattribution, structurally similar to the 'Manhattan' joke. This one works slightly less well because it's a bit more predictable, but 'the good times you have when you're in it' is a genuinely funny wrong answer — it sounds like folk etymology Michael might actually believe.

jokes.text: Michael's Times Square restaurant recommendations: 'Great places to eat. We have Bubba Gump Shrimp, Red Lobster down there.'
jokes.setup: Michael is presenting himself as a Times Square connoisseur with insider knowledge of great dining
jokes.punchline: His 'great places to eat' are tourist-trap chain restaurants — Bubba Gump Shrimp and Red Lobster — presented with complete local authority
jokes.explanation: The specific choices of Bubba Gump Shrimp and Red Lobster are well-chosen — they're not random bad restaurants but specifically the kind of chain restaurants that real New Yorkers find embarrassing and tourists gravitate to. Michael presenting these as insider tips is precise satire of his particular brand of oblivious confidence.

jokes.text: Phyllis receives another enormous delivery from Bob Vance. Kevin: 'Holy God. It's from Bob. Man, that thing's bigger than I am.'
jokes.setup: Phyllis already received one gift from Bob. Another, apparently enormous, delivery arrives.
jokes.punchline: Kevin's 'Holy God' and 'that thing's bigger than I am' — the escalating absurdity of Bob Vance's romantic excess
jokes.explanation: Escalation of the Bob Vance running gag. Works because Kevin's reaction (complete awe) and Phyllis's defensive 'Oh, zip it' are both in character. The visual of the enormous gift is inferred but clearly the point. Sets up later Pam/Roy conversation about gift envy.

jokes.text: Michael narrating the subway: 'Everybody takes the subway in New York. It's fast, it's efficient, gets you there on time.' — then interrupts himself mid-sentence when he sees a man pooping in a cardboard box.
jokes.setup: Michael is confidently extolling the New York subway as a sophisticated transit system, performing his local-New-Yorker persona
jokes.punchline: 'It's a way to... Okay, there's a guy pooping in a cardboard box down there.' — mid-sentence collapse of the confident narration, replaced by startled reportage
jokes.explanation: The structure is excellent — the abandoned sentence 'It's a way to...' followed immediately by the report is perfectly timed. The joke works because Michael is mid-performance of New York sophistication and reality intrudes brutally. 'In a cardboard box' is a specific detail that elevates it above a generic 'gross subway' joke.

jokes.text: Michael at Rockefeller Center: 'Founded, of course, by Theodore Rockefeller.'
jokes.setup: Michael is giving a confident tour of Rockefeller Center as a New York insider
jokes.punchline: 'Theodore Rockefeller' — the Rockefeller family patriarch was John D. Rockefeller; Michael's confident wrong first name ('Theodore') shows he knows enough to be wrong specifically
jokes.explanation: Part of the Michael-as-confident-ignoramus tour sequence. 'Theodore' is a funny specific wrong name. Works as accumulation with the other tour gags rather than as a standout joke on its own.

jokes.text: Michael spots Tina Fey: 'And it's... that's Tina Fey. That's Tina Fey from Saturday Night Live.' — then approaches her and she rebuffs him.
jokes.setup: Michael is touring Rockefeller Center (where NBC/SNL is filmed) and spots a woman he thinks is Tina Fey
jokes.punchline: Michael approaches her confidently, she clearly isn't Tina Fey (or is and wants nothing to do with him), and Michael retreats: 'She looked like... she looked a lot like Tina Fey' — compounded when he apparently also missed a celebrity encounter while talking to the wrong person
jokes.explanation: The NBC/SNL meta-reference (the show films at 30 Rock) is a nice layer. The compounding failure — he approached the wrong person AND missed the real celebrity — is good escalation. The 'She looked a lot like Tina Fey' excuse delivered directly to camera is a nice reaction beat.

jokes.text: Michael on the phone, apparently just missing a second celebrity sighting while distracted by the fake Tina Fey: 'When? When I was talking to the fake Tina Fey? Come on!'
jokes.setup: Michael just approached and was rejected by a Tina Fey lookalike
jokes.punchline: He simultaneously learns he missed a real celebrity encounter because of the fake Tina Fey distraction — a perfect comedic compounding of failure
jokes.explanation: 'When I was talking to the fake Tina Fey?' is a great line — the phrase 'fake Tina Fey' is unexpected and funny as a category. The compounding failure structure works well. Slightly undermined by uncertainty about who the real missed celebrity was, but the escalation lands.

jokes.text: Angela and the mystery gift-giver: 'Did you hear? Somebody totally rocked the house and got me the best present I've ever gotten.' 'I wouldn't know anything about that. But I'm glad you enjoyed it.'
jokes.setup: Angela has received an amazing Valentine's gift and is telling someone about it; we're waiting to see if the giver reveals themselves
jokes.punchline: The conversation reveals Dwight is the giver (they're secretly dating) but both maintain absurd deniability while clearly communicating — 'I wouldn't know anything about that' is their version of romantic code
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Angela and Dwight are conducting a romance through the grammar of denial. 'I wouldn't know anything about that' is a funny specific line — it's what someone would say if they were completely innocent, not someone who's happy their gift was well-received. The audience knows they're a couple, so the performance of ignorance is the comedy.

jokes.text: Michael's New York fantasy: 'Scranton is great, but New York is like Scranton on acid.'
jokes.setup: Michael is describing his dream of living in New York and working corporate
jokes.punchline: 'New York is like Scranton on acid' — the comparison is backwards (Scranton is a smaller version of NY, not the baseline) but Michael's framing makes Scranton the reference point for reality
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely quotable and original line. The joke operates on multiple levels: the absurdity of using Scranton as the baseline, Michael's unironic pride in both cities, and the specific choice of 'acid' as the intensifier. Then Michael second-guesses himself ('No, on speed. Nah. On steroids.') which is almost funnier — he's workshopping the metaphor in real time and settling on something less interesting. Just shy of 8+ because the self-correction undercuts the original punch.

jokes.text: Michael's Desert Storm analogy for his presentation: 'It's like Michael Jordan in the NBA finals or like Stormin' Norman Schwarzkopf. And this presentation is Desert Storm. And as soon as it's over, we will not have to deal with those Iraqis anymore.'
jokes.setup: Michael is psyching himself up before his big presentation to the CFO
jokes.punchline: The analogy collapses — Michael starts comparing himself to Michael Jordan (flattering), pivots to Schwarzkopf/Desert Storm (oddly specific), and then extends the metaphor to saying the CFO/corporate review is 'the Iraqis' — making the people judging him the enemy in a war analogy
jokes.explanation: The joke escalates well — Jordan is a common sports comparison, Schwarzkopf is already odd, and then the Iraqis extension is the logical (absurd) completion. The joke reveals Michael frames every interaction as a military conquest, and that he's probably going to approach his corporate presentation with the wrong energy.

jokes.text: Michael's introduction of Craig: 'You have been kicked out of every strip club in Albany, is that true?' Craig: 'Guilty.'
jokes.setup: Michael is networking with branch managers before the CFO meeting
jokes.punchline: Michael's 'introduction' of Craig is a boast about his strip club ejections, delivered as if this is a charming credential
jokes.explanation: Good reveal of Michael's social world — this is how he bonds with male colleagues. The detail of Albany specifically is funny (modest strip club credentials). Craig's proud 'Guilty' confirms they both think this is fine. Character world-building.

jokes.text: Pam warns Dwight: 'You can't fire me, Dwight, just 'cause Michael's not here.' Dwight: 'No, Pam, just, um...'
jokes.setup: Dwight has asked to speak with Pam privately while Michael is away
jokes.punchline: Pam immediately and correctly identifies that Dwight's private conversations often involve attempts to assert authority — then Dwight's stammering reveals he actually has a vulnerable, non-authoritarian purpose (needing Valentine's Day advice)
jokes.explanation: Good character joke — Pam's read of Dwight is accurate and funny, but then the subversion (he needs help with romance) makes Pam's defensive posture retroactively amusing. The pivot to Dwight being vulnerable is a good setup for the next scene.

jokes.text: Dwight describes his girlfriend to Pam without naming her: 'She's not really the kind of person you'd think would be into Valentine's Day. She's kind of...' Pam: 'Tightly wound?'
jokes.setup: Dwight is cryptically describing his mystery Valentine without revealing her identity
jokes.punchline: Pam immediately and correctly identifies the mystery girlfriend as 'tightly wound' — which is an extremely apt description of Angela — without knowing who it is; she just knows one type of person Dwight would date
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Pam's guess is both correct and reveals her accurate read of Dwight's type. 'Tightly wound' is a perfect euphemism for Angela. Dwight's immediate 'Exactly' without catching that Pam has basically identified his girlfriend is good character comedy — he's so focused on his problem he doesn't notice the near-exposure.

jokes.text: Pam: 'Sometimes the gift is really about the gesture... instead of what it is.' Dwight: 'You mean like a ham?'
jokes.setup: Pam is giving Dwight earnest relationship advice about romantic gestures
jokes.punchline: 'You mean like a ham?' — Dwight has processed Pam's abstract concept of a meaningful gesture and arrived at a smoked meat product as the logical example
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's funniest joke. 'You mean like a ham?' is perfect in every dimension. The setup is sincere and well-established — Pam is genuinely trying to help. The punchline arrives with no warning and is utterly specific: not 'a gift,' not 'food,' but a ham — which is simultaneously a classic gift (Dwight is farm-raised and practical), a gesture (it's substantial), and completely wrong as a romantic token. Pam's defeated 'No. Not like a ham.' is the ideal straight-man response. The joke earns its 8+ through exceptional economy (four words that couldn't be improved), complete character specificity (only Dwight goes to ham), and the perfect subversion of the sincere setup. One of the best jokes in this episode.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'Okay, shut up. I know exactly what to do.' — after Pam says it's about caring, not what the gift is
jokes.setup: Pam has given Dwight romantic advice, and he claims to understand
jokes.punchline: 'Okay, shut up. I know exactly what to do' — Dwight's pivot from requesting help to immediately dismissing the helper once he thinks he has what he needs; his gratitude is indistinguishable from rudeness
jokes.explanation: A character-specific punchline to the scene — Dwight's 'shut up' to Pam is both rude and weirdly endearing because it's clearly not hostile, just his mode of operation. Works as a scene-ender.

jokes.text: Craig describes ignoring Jan's order to fire four people: 'She called me in September. And she's like, you gotta fire four people. And I was just like, what? You know.' 'Did you?' 'No. I just ignored her.'
jokes.setup: Michael and fellow branch managers are chatting before the CFO presentation, bonding over their shared boss Jan
jokes.punchline: Craig casually reveals he just ignored a direct order from a senior executive to fire four people — as if it were a reasonable option
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the casualness of Craig's dereliction — 'I just ignored her' delivered without any sense that this is unusual behavior. Sets up Craig as reckless and explains his later presentation-free appearance before the CFO.

jokes.text: Craig: 'She is the worst.' Michael: 'She is our boss.' Craig: 'She ain't my boss, dude. I don't work for that bitch.' Michael: 'Hey, ca... ca... come on... maybe because she's my girlfriend.'
jokes.setup: Craig is badmouthing Jan while Michael is trying to politely defend her; the audience might expect Michael to defend Jan professionally
jokes.punchline: Michael's actual reason for defending Jan is that she's his girlfriend — a reveal that recontextualizes all his hedging and is deeply awkward given Craig's language
jokes.explanation: The timing of Michael's reveal ('maybe because she's my girlfriend') lands hard because of what Craig just called her. Michael's stuttering lead-up ('ca... ca... come on') shows him trying to find a way to de-escalate before resorting to the truth. The reveal is both funny and humanizing — Michael is defending Jan's honor even while their relationship is officially over.

jokes.text: Michael's 'Was or not my girlfriend' correction and the awkward revelation that he and Jan hooked up, which Craig didn't know.
jokes.setup: Michael just revealed Jan is his girlfriend in front of other branch managers
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately backtracks ('Was or not my girlfriend'), admits it was 'just once,' and the whole thing becomes maximally uncomfortable — culminating in 'Just forget it'
jokes.explanation: The cringe value is high — Michael's backpedaling is characteristically disastrous. The scene functions well as a slow-motion overshare. Not as cleanly structured as the best jokes but effective cringe comedy.

jokes.text: Kelly's talking head about Ryan: 'I don't know what he's thinking, but I would just be so psyched if we just dated forever.'
jokes.setup: Kelly and Ryan literally just hooked up for the first time (on February 13th, per Ryan's correction)
jokes.punchline: Kelly has already escalated to 'dated forever' — complete commitment in one step, from first kiss to imagining marriage
jokes.explanation: Standard Kelly hyperbole, very much in character — she operates at full romantic intensity always. Works as part of the Kelly/Ryan arc but isn't a standout joke on its own.

jokes.text: Ryan to Kelly: 'I mean, I know that it's Valentine's Day or whatever, but there's totally no pressure at all of any kind whatsoever.'
jokes.setup: Ryan is asking Kelly out on Valentine's Day
jokes.punchline: 'Valentine's Day or whatever' — Ryan's studied indifference to the holiday's romantic significance, then the over-correction of 'no pressure at all of any kind whatsoever' which is three redundant reassurances that actually create pressure
jokes.explanation: 'Valentine's Day or whatever' is a great Ryan line — the casual dismissal is exactly his brand. Then 'of any kind whatsoever' is the tell that he's protesting too much. The escalating denial structure is well-observed.

jokes.text: Kelly declines Ryan's invitation because she has plans — Jim's poker game — and Ryan's visible non-reaction / the beat of awkward politeness between them.
jokes.setup: Ryan has asked Kelly out on Valentine's Day while claiming there's no pressure
jokes.punchline: Kelly turns him down. Ryan says 'That's cool. I completely understand. Okay. Cool.' — three acknowledgments of being fine, suggesting he's absolutely not fine but committed to his no-pressure persona
jokes.explanation: The triple 'Okay. Cool. / Okay. Cool.' is a nice character beat — Ryan repeating himself reveals the crack in his indifferent facade. Functional cringe comedy.

jokes.text: Jan's talking head: 'And, well, it is Michael. So, yeah, I'm very nervous.'
jokes.setup: Jan is describing the pressure of Michael's presentation to the new CFO
jokes.punchline: 'And, well, it is Michael. So, yeah, I'm very nervous.' — Jan's exhausted, resigned acknowledgment that Michael being Michael is sufficient reason to be extremely anxious
jokes.explanation: Jan's exhaustion with Michael is a running vein of comedy, and 'it is Michael' as sufficient explanation for maximum anxiety is a clean, economical expression of their dynamic. The pause before 'I'm very nervous' lets the understatement land.

jokes.text: Michael's presentation begins: 'What is a business? Is it a collection of numbers and sales reports? Sure.' Then cuts to a video montage.
jokes.setup: Michael is supposed to give a financial presentation to the CFO
jokes.punchline: 'Sure' — Michael's rhetorical question about business gets an immediate concessive answer that he then ignores. He has made a video instead of a financial report, and 'sure' acknowledges the correct answer before dismissing it
jokes.explanation: The single word 'Sure' after the rhetorical question is excellent — it collapses Michael's attempted profundity before he can get going. Then he pivots to his video anyway. The joke anticipates the cringe of the presentation that follows.

jokes.text: Michael begins his presentation: 'What is a business? Is it a collection of numbers and sales reports?' [Long pause.] 'Sure.'
jokes.setup: Michael begins what was supposed to be a financial presentation with a rhetorical philosophical question
jokes.punchline: 'Sure' — after posing a grand rhetorical question about the nature of business, Michael immediately concedes the boring, literal answer, undermining his own opening
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional comedy writing. The rhetorical setup — 'What is a business? Is it a collection of numbers and sales reports?' — sounds like it's building to something profound. The one-word concession 'Sure' is a total collapse that is both extremely funny and completely Michael: he builds to the dramatic, then immediately gives way because he can't actually argue against the obvious answer. Perfect economy. Justifies 8+ because this is a structurally brilliant subversion.

jokes.text: Michael's video: 'Life moves a little slower in Scranton, Pennsylvania. And that's the way we like it.' — accompanied by presumably slow, pastoral footage of Scranton.
jokes.setup: Michael is showing a corporate financial presentation to a new CFO
jokes.punchline: The presentation appears to be a lifestyle documentary about Scranton rather than financial data — Michael has made a promotional video for a regional paper company instead of a financial report
jokes.explanation: The joke builds as we realize the scope of Michael's misunderstanding — this isn't a brief intro, it's his entire presentation. 'Life moves a little slower in Scranton. And that's the way we like it' is written in the cadence of a tourism commercial, which is the wrong genre for a CFO meeting.

jokes.text: Michael's video narrates Stanley: 'An African-American father of two, Stanley's dedication is no doubt one of the hallmarks of the foundation of the business we're hoping to build our basis on.'
jokes.setup: Michael is showcasing employees in his presentation video
jokes.punchline: The description of Stanley leads with 'African-American' — an awkward, unnecessary racial qualifier in an ostensible business presentation — followed by a sentence that means almost nothing ('hallmarks of the foundation of the business we're hoping to build our basis on')
jokes.explanation: Michael's inclusion of Stanley's race in the introduction is the kind of well-meaning-but-cringe mistake that's very characteristic of the show. The subsequent word salad ('hallmarks of the foundation of the business we're hoping to build our basis on') is meaningless corporate-speak that Michael clearly finds impressive. Double cringe.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head about the video: 'Yeah, I shot a bunch of footage around the office, edited it together on my Mac. Was thinking about entering it in some festivals. Probably won't. You know, not what this is about.'
jokes.setup: Michael explains his approach to the CFO presentation
jokes.punchline: He casually mentions he was going to enter his corporate video in film festivals — revealing the whole thing is a vanity project — then catches himself: 'Probably won't. You know, not what this is about.'
jokes.explanation: Michael's self-correction ('Probably won't. You know, not what this is about.') is funnier than the festival ambition because it shows a flicker of self-awareness immediately smothered. The pause before 'probably won't' does real work. Good character economy.

jokes.text: Michael's video ending: 'What it's like to walk a mile in Oscar's shoes. Or try on Phyllis' pants.'
jokes.setup: Michael is wrapping up his corporate video with inspirational language
jokes.punchline: 'Or try on Phyllis' pants' — the idiom 'walk a mile in someone's shoes' gets an escalation to 'try on Phyllis' pants' which is both a size joke and a complete collapse of Michael's attempted profundity
jokes.explanation: A well-structured joke — Michael establishes the idiom correctly with Oscar's shoes, then extends it in the most awkward possible direction with Phyllis' pants. It's simultaneously a body-shaming joke Michael doesn't realize is a body-shaming joke and a destruction of his own rhetorical momentum. Characteristically Michael.

jokes.text: 'Great Scott!' — David (the CFO) says as Michael's presentation ends, then immediately pivots to: 'Questions.'
jokes.setup: Michael's catastrophic video presentation has just finished; the CFO has sat through the whole thing
jokes.punchline: 'Great Scott!' (possibly a Sherlock Holmes/Back to the Future reference, possibly genuine surprise, possibly both) followed immediately by the most professional possible pivot to 'Questions' — the CFO is processing and moving on
jokes.explanation: The pause between the exclamation and 'Questions' is where the joke lives — the CFO collecting himself. 'Great Scott' as an exclamation is simultaneously period-appropriate executive speech and an inadvertent reference to Michael's name. The pivot to professional mode is the punchline.

jokes.text: Oscar at the reception desk receives nothing for Valentine's Day. Kevin's advice: 'Nothing for me? Join the club.' Followed by Oscar: 'Who's it from?' About his gift. 'My mom.'
jokes.setup: Valentine's Day gifts have been arriving at the office all day
jokes.punchline: Oscar's gift is from his mom — the most deflating possible Valentine's Day reveal for an adult
jokes.explanation: The mom reveal is a well-worn Valentine's Day joke — receiving a gift from your mother — but it's delivered efficiently. Kevin's 'Join the club' adds a nice beat. Functional but not inventive.

jokes.text: Jim invites Kelly to his poker game to cheer her up. Kelly: 'Okay, cool. Is it okay if I invite Ryan?'
jokes.setup: Jim is trying to help Kelly move on from Ryan by inviting her to his card game
jokes.punchline: Kelly immediately asks to bring Ryan — completely defeating the purpose of the invitation to move on
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the gap between Jim's intention (help Kelly move on) and Kelly's response (immediately reinserting Ryan). Well-timed, character-specific, and gets Jim's helpless reaction as an implied punchline.

jokes.text: Craig's explanation for having no financial presentation: 'I was under the impression this was more of like a meet-and-greet type deal.'
jokes.setup: Craig has shown up to a formal 'financial presentation' with no financial data
jokes.punchline: 'I was under the impression this was more of like a meet-and-greet type deal' — Craig's interpretation of 'financial presentation' as a social event is either spectacular delusion or spectacular laziness
jokes.explanation: The CFO's response ('What did you think 'financial presentation' meant?') is the ideal straight-man line, and Craig's answer is comically specific — not 'I didn't understand' but the precise wrong interpretation of 'meet-and-greet.' Sets up the later Jan payoff.

jokes.text: Craig blames Michael's video: 'You know what? Michael made that stupid movie. He doesn't get in any trouble. Maybe I should've slept with you too.'
jokes.setup: Craig is being dressed down for having no presentation while Michael apparently got away with his video
jokes.punchline: 'Maybe I should've slept with you too' — Craig says this to Jan in front of the CFO, a career-ending, jaw-dropping non-sequitur that reveals Michael's earlier overshare has spread
jokes.explanation: This is an extremely well-constructed callback. Craig's casual 'Maybe I should've slept with you too' lands as a bomb — the audience has been waiting for the consequence of Michael's overshare, and Craig delivers it in the worst possible setting (to Jan's face, in front of the CFO). The 'too' is what makes it — it implies the action is on the table as a general career strategy. Jan's silent horror and Michael's panic are the implied reaction. Strong callback payoff.

jokes.text: Jan to Michael after the Craig disaster: 'I just don't know what to do anymore, Michael.'
jokes.setup: Michael and Jan are alone after the CFO meeting where Craig implied Jan sleeps her way through management
jokes.punchline: Jan's line — 'I just don't know what to do anymore' — has layers: it's professionally about the Craig situation, personally about Michael, and existentially about her entire relationship with the Scranton branch. Her exhaustion is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Jan's exhaustion functions as both comedy and pathos — the show's particular strength. Not a big laugh moment but part of the sustained cringe of the New York storyline.

jokes.text: Jan: 'The CFO thinks that we slept together.' Michael: 'Technically, we fell asleep in the same bed.'
jokes.setup: Jan is panicking that the CFO believes they had an affair
jokes.punchline: Michael's lawyerly correction — 'Technically, we fell asleep in the same bed' — as if the technical distinction matters, and as if 'we fell asleep in the same bed' is significantly less compromising than what Jan said
jokes.explanation: 'Technically, we fell asleep in the same bed' is a strong Michael line because the qualifier 'technically' implies he thinks he's making a meaningful distinction when he's actually confirming the scandal. The deadpan insistence on precision in an imprecise social situation is very Michael. Near 8-territory for structure and character integration.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Surely, you cannot be serious.' Jan: [presumably mortified] Michael: 'I am serious, and don't call me Shirley. Airplane.'
jokes.setup: Michael promises to fix the situation with the CFO; Jan expresses disbelief
jokes.punchline: Michael delivers the famous Airplane! quote ('I am serious, and don't call me Shirley') and then immediately cites the source — 'Airplane.' — as if Jan might not have recognized it
jokes.explanation: The joke is not in the quote itself (which is very well-known) but in Michael's citation — 'Airplane.' — delivered as if he's attributing a quote in an academic paper. The need to explain the reference to Jan in this moment is perfectly Michael: he can't resist a bit even in a crisis, and he doesn't trust people to recognize his references.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head: 'Women are like wolves. If you want a wolf, you have to trap it. You have to snare it. And then you have to tame it. Keep it happy. Care for it. Feed it. Lovingly the way an animal deserves to be loved. And my animal deserves a lot of loving.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is describing his philosophy on romantic relationships after his Valentine's advice session with Pam
jokes.punchline: The wolf metaphor begins aggressively (trap, snare, tame) but softens into genuine affection ('lovingly the way an animal deserves to be loved') and then pivots back to something vaguely menacing with 'my animal deserves a lot of loving' — Dwight's romance philosophy is simultaneously caveman and sincere
jokes.explanation: This is a strong character monologue because it contains its own internal arc — aggressive hunting metaphor → genuine tenderness → ambiguous conclusion. 'My animal deserves a lot of loving' is somehow both sweet and disturbing. Only Dwight would frame romance as wildlife management. High character integration score because no other character on the show would say anything like this.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'Women are like wolves. If you want a wolf, you have to trap it. You have to snare it. And then you have to tame it. Keep it happy. Care for it. Feed it. Lovingly the way an animal deserves to be loved. And my animal deserves a lot of loving.'
jokes.setup: Michael is sharing his philosophy of romantic relationships in a talking head
jokes.punchline: The wolf metaphor escalates through increasingly specific animal-husbandry steps and ends with 'my animal deserves a lot of loving' — Michael has not noticed that calling Jan 'my animal' is not romantic
jokes.explanation: Michael's romantic worldview rendered as predatory wildlife management is a rich extended metaphor. 'My animal deserves a lot of loving' is the peak — he's completely unaware of how disturbing this sounds. Strong character integration; this is Michael's genuine belief about love.

jokes.text: Pam tells Roy she'd hoped he'd get her something despite their 'no big gifts' agreement — Roy's response: 'Valentine's Day isn't over. Let's get you home, and you are gonna get the best sex of your life.'
jokes.setup: Pam has spent the day watching Bob Vance shower Phyllis with enormous romantic gifts and now confesses she wished Roy had gotten her something
jokes.punchline: Roy's Valentine's Day gift to Pam is a promise of sex — delivered with genuine enthusiasm but completely missing that Pam wanted to feel valued and seen, not propositioned
jokes.explanation: Roy's response is perfect character economy — he's not mean, he's simply operating from a completely different emotional register. 'The best sex of your life' is delivered as a genuine attempt at a gift, which makes Pam's quiet disappointment (and the audience's recognition of the incompatibility) the real punchline. The context of Bob Vance's lavish gestures makes this land harder.

jokes.text: Michael explaining Craig's comment to David: 'Before you guys came in, I was talking to the guys, we were all chatting. And I made a joke. A really dumb joke. And Craig the idiot took it seriously.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to explain away Craig's 'maybe I should've slept with you too' comment
jokes.punchline: 'Craig the idiot' — Michael is describing himself as the victim of Craig's misunderstanding while the audience knows Michael created the entire situation by oversharing
jokes.explanation: Michael blaming 'Craig the idiot' while he is the idiot in this scenario is classic Michael — complete inversion of responsibility with sincere conviction. Functional but not the strongest version of this joke type.

jokes.text: Michael defending Jan to the CFO: 'Jan is a fantastic executive and has all the integrity in the world.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to clear Jan's name with the CFO after Craig's implication
jokes.punchline: Michael is defending Jan's integrity after having told multiple branch managers he slept with her — the irony of Michael as character witness for Jan's professionalism is thick
jokes.explanation: The joke is entirely in context — Michael as integrity's defender after causing the integrity crisis. Works as a beat in the larger scene rather than a standalone joke.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam's goodbye: 'Heading out?' 'Yeah.' 'All right, Beesly.' 'Hey, happy Valentine's Day.' 'Bye.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam are saying goodbye at the end of the Valentine's Day workday; Jim asked her out (implied) earlier and she declined, he's now single and clearly has feelings for her
jokes.punchline: The entire goodbye is almost nothing — two people who have feelings for each other saying the least meaningful possible words on the most romantic day of the year. The comedy/pathos lives in what isn't said.
jokes.explanation: This qualifies for an 8+ score because of exceptional economy and character integration. The joke — if it can be called that — is the vast emotional gulf between what Jim and Pam feel and what they say: 'All right, Beesly' / 'Hey, happy Valentine's Day' / 'Bye.' In the context of the episode's Valentine's Day theme, surrounded by Bob Vance's lavish gestures and Roy's obliviousness, this non-moment is devastating and funny in equal measure. It's The Office at its best: the comedy is entirely in the absence of what should be said. Only these two characters could make this exchange resonate this way.

jokes.text: Jan thanks Michael for defending her to the CFO. Moment of genuine warmth. Then: 'So, uh, happy Valentine's Day.' 'Yeah, happy Valentine's Day.' — beat of longing between them.
jokes.setup: Michael and Jan have just navigated a crisis together that Michael caused; Jan is grateful
jokes.punchline: The Valentine's Day exchange — after everything, after Jan's morning email telling Michael to back off, after the CFO meeting disaster — they're alone in New York on Valentine's Day saying 'happy Valentine's Day' to each other with an enormous unspoken situation between them
jokes.explanation: The double 'happy Valentine's Day' exchange is the episode's thematic button — it calls back to Jan's morning email, the whole New York adventure, and Michael's doomed romantic impulses. The comedy is the formality of 'Happy Valentine's Day' as two people who have complicated feelings try to observe the holiday professionally. The subsequent pause [20:25] amplifies it.

jokes.text: The long pause after the 'Happy Valentine's Day' exchange between Michael and Jan — inferred from [20:07] to [20:31] timestamp gap — before the scene ends
jokes.setup: Michael and Jan have exchanged Valentine's Day greetings; neither moves; the situation is full of unspoken meaning
jokes.punchline: The silence itself — two people caught in a moment that neither can resolve — is the joke/pathos. Someone likely makes a small involuntary sound or gesture.
jokes.explanation: The silence after the exchange functions as its own joke — the episode has been about Valentine's Day, romantic gestures, connections made and missed, and it ends on two people unable to say what they mean on the one day designed for exactly that. The 'Oh.' [20:25] suggests one of them breaks first with a small, deflating sound. The show's command of the silent beat is a signature strength.

jokes.text: Final moment/tag: 'Oi vey... schmear.' — Michael apparently saying something Jewish-inflected as a parting comment in New York
jokes.setup: The episode is ending in New York after all of Michael's tourist adventures
jokes.punchline: 'Oi vey... schmear' — Michael appropriating New York Jewish vernacular as a parting shot, delivered apparently to no one, as if absorbing the city's culture into himself
jokes.explanation: 'Schmear' after 'Oi vey' is the funny specific wrong word — 'oi vey' is an expression of exasperation, and Michael adds 'schmear' (cream cheese, a bagel topping) as if completing the phrase. It's Michael trying on New York Jewish identity like a tourist souvenir. Slight joke to end on — more charming than hilarious.

jokes.text: Jan's final muttered line: 'Oi vey... schmear.'
jokes.setup: Jan has just had an emotionally complex Valentine's Day — her professional reputation was nearly destroyed and she and Michael shared a genuine moment
jokes.punchline: 'Oi vey... schmear' — a Yiddish exclamation of exasperation followed by 'schmear' (to spread/mess) — Jan summarizing her feelings about Michael in a private mutter as the elevator closes
jokes.explanation: Jan allowing herself one unguarded, self-aware moment — 'Oi vey... schmear' — is a perfect character-specific ending. It's funny because Jan is usually so composed; the Yiddish idiom suggests her actual feelings peeking through corporate polish. The word 'schmear' also has the double meaning of 'mess' (her situation) and bagel schmear — which would be exactly the kind of New York callback that fits this episode.

tmdb_overview: The Dunder-Mifflin staffers join in kindergarten-like festivities for Valentine's Day while Michael heads to New York City for a conference with the corporate heads. After showing the documenters a tour of his favorite city, Michael accidentally lets slip to the others at the conference that he and Jan hooked up, and he finds himself in hot water when Jan and the new CFO of Dunder-Mifflin hear the story. Back in Scranton, Pam becomes irked when she discovers that Roy hasn't gotten her anything for Valentine's Day, Dwight struggles to find a gift for Angela, and Kelley talks off Jim's ear about her rather desperate affections for Ryan, who is less than interested.
